passage: The ice-cream cart rang its bell at the gate of Sunrise Colony, and a dozen kids ran for it. Imran was first in line when Usha squeezed in front, her elbow knocking his arm. "Hey! You're so rude," he shouted. "Always pushing." Usha pointed at her building. "Mummy's calling me for dinner, I only have one minute!" Imran didn't hear that part. The next evening Imran was the one running late for his tabla class. He shoved past two kids at the cart, grabbed his cone and ran. "Sorry, sorry, I'm late!" he called over his shoulder, feeling perfectly reasonable. That night he told his father, "Usha pushes because she's rude. I only pushed because I had tabla." His father looked at him for a long moment.

qa.q: Why was Imran in a hurry the next evening?
qa.a: Imran was running late for his tabla class.

qa.q: Why did Imran feel perfectly reasonable shoving past the kids?
qa.a: Imran felt comfortable with his own push because he knew all about his late tabla class, while Usha's reason never reached him.

qa.q: What could Imran's father ask to help him?
qa.a: His father could ask, 'What did Usha say when she pushed?' so Imran remembers that her mummy was calling her too.

qa.q: How might the two kids Imran shoved see him?
qa.a: They only saw a boy pushing past them, so they might call him rude, just as Imran called Usha.

grounding: A boy excuses his own push by his hurry but calls a girl's push rude, ignoring that she was in a hurry too.

passage:
"You pushed me off the swing!" Noor said, brushing sand off her knees.
"I didn't push. I just needed a turn fast. The bell was about to ring," said Thomas.
"So? Yesterday when Kiran pushed you off the slide, you said he was a bully."
"Because he is. He pushes everyone."
"And you pushed me."
"That's different. I had a reason."
"Maybe Kiran had a reason too."
"Like what?"
Noor shrugged. "Maybe the bell was about to ring for him too."
Thomas kicked at the sand. "His reason is he's mean."
"And your reason is the bell?"
"Yes."
Noor climbed back onto the swing. "Then I'm keeping it, because the bell hasn't rung."

qa.q: Why does Thomas say Noor was pushed off the swing?
qa.a: Thomas says the push was only about needing a turn fast because the bell was about to ring.

qa.q: Why does Thomas think that push is different from Kiran's?
qa.a: Thomas feels that rush from inside, so that push has a reason, while Kiran is only seen from outside, so Kiran's push gets called mean.

qa.q: What could Thomas try when he wants to call someone a bully?
qa.a: Thomas could ask what reason Kiran might have had, just as Thomas had one.

qa.q: How does Noor see the two pushes?
qa.a: Noor sees them as the same kind of push and wonders why only Thomas gets to have a reason.

grounding: A child says their own push came from being rushed but a classmate's push came from being mean.

passage: I'm Ronak, and this happened in the morning assembly line. Shreya pushed me from behind and I nearly fell on the boy in front. I told Manjula Miss, "Shreya is rude. She always pushes." Then, when the line moved to our classroom, I pushed Deepu so I could get the window seat before anyone else. Manjula Miss said, "Good boys don't push, Ronak." I said I was in a hurry because my bag was so heavy. Later I found out Shreya had been pushed by the big boys behind her. I felt a bit silly. My push had a reason, but I never asked about hers. Now I think maybe she had a reason too.

qa.q: Why did Ronak push Deepu?
qa.a: He pushed Deepu so he could get the window seat before anyone else.

qa.q: How did Ronak feel after learning why Shreya pushed?
qa.a: He felt a bit silly, because his own push had a reason but he never asked about hers.

qa.q: What would you advise Ronak when someone pushes him in the line?
qa.a: Before calling them rude, he could look behind them or ask what happened, since someone might be pushing them too.

qa.q: How might Deepu feel about being pushed for the window seat?
qa.a: Deepu might think Ronak is rude, just as Ronak thought about Shreya, because Deepu can't see the heavy bag.

grounding: A boy blames a classmate's rudeness for her push while excusing his own push by his hurry.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Seema, Class 3B, Monday.
In the lunch rush today, Jomon pushed Deepak aside to reach the tap. Deepak scraped his elbow on the wall. When I asked Jomon what happened, he said quickly, "I had to push, Miss, the bell was ringing and I was so thirsty."
Later, in class, he complained, "Deepak pushed me in the morning line! He's so rude. He always does rude things."
I asked him whether Deepak might have been in a hurry too. "No, he's just rude."
What I did next: I sat both boys together after lunch, asked each to tell me why they pushed. Both said, "I was in a hurry." Jomon looked at Deepak with his mouth open. I have moved the tap queue earlier so it isn't a rush.

qa.q: What did Deepak scrape when he fell against the wall?
qa.a: Deepak scraped his elbow.

qa.q: Why did Jomon feel his own push was fine but Deepak's push was rude?
qa.a: Jomon was annoyed at Deepak but felt his own push had a reason, because he could feel his own hurry and thirst but not Deepak's, so Deepak's push seemed to come from being a rude person.

qa.q: What did Seema do after lunch, and what did Jomon discover?
qa.a: She sat both boys together and asked why each had pushed, and Jomon heard Deepak give the same reason, being in a hurry, which surprised him.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt about being called rude by Jomon?
qa.a: Deepak probably felt it was unfair, since he had also just been rushing, and he had been the one who got hurt at the tap.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a boy explaining his own push by a hurry while calling another child's push rude.

passage:
Thursday
Today in the school bus line Ojas pushed me so hard my bag fell in a puddle. Ojas is SO rude. He always pushes. He never says sorry. I don't like him at all.
Then in the evening, at the park, the ice cream man was leaving and I ran and I pushed a small girl out of the way. She cried a little bit. But that was not my fault, the ice cream man was going and I had to be fast. Anyone would push.
Mummy asked if Ojas was maybe rushing for the bus. I said no, because he is just like that. Then Mummy said, "And you were just like that at the park, my boy?" and I said NO, because I had a reason.
I don't think Mummy understands. Also my ice cream was mango.
Harish

qa.q: Where did Harish's bag fall when Ojas pushed him?
qa.a: His bag fell in a puddle.

qa.q: Why does Harish feel his own push at the park was not his fault?
qa.a: Harish felt annoyed at Ojas but saw his own push as fair, since he knew he was rushing for the ice cream man, while Ojas's push seemed to show that Ojas is a rude person.

qa.q: What question could Mummy ask next to help Harish see both pushes more evenly?
qa.a: She could ask what Ojas might have been rushing for, the way Harish rushed for the ice cream, so Harish works out on his own that both had reasons.

qa.q: How might the small girl at the park see Harish's push?
qa.a: To the small girl it probably felt just as rude as Ojas's push felt to Harish, since she only saw a big kid shove her and did not know about the ice cream man leaving.

grounding: A boy's diary shows him explaining his own push by hurry while calling another boy's push a sign of being rude.

passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, Wednesday, after assembly
At the water cooler this morning, Kunal and Ankita both pushed in the line, a few minutes apart. When I spoke to Kunal, he said, "I only pushed because the bell was ringing and I was late for PE." Ten minutes later, when Ankita pushed him, he came to me red-faced: "Ankita pushed me because she's rude. She's always rude." When I asked whether Ankita might have been in a hurry too, he said, "No, she's just like that." I asked him to think about what he had told me about the bell. He was quiet, then said, "Maybe she had PE too." Both children apologised. I will talk to the class about queues on Friday.

qa.q: Why did Kunal say he pushed?
qa.a: Because the bell was ringing and he was late for PE.

qa.q: Why did Kunal think Ankita pushed because she is rude?
qa.a: He felt upset and hurt at being pushed, so it seemed like her character, while his own push felt like it had a good reason.

qa.q: What question did the teacher ask that helped, and why?
qa.a: Whether Ankita might have been in a hurry too, which reminded Kunal of his own bell reason so he could see she might have one.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel being called always rude?
qa.a: Ankita might feel hurt and unfairly labelled, especially if she was rushing too.

grounding: A teacher records a boy explaining his own push by the bell but another child's push by rudeness.

passage:
Sunday
Vidya didi shouted at me today for using her headphones. She is SO rude. She's always rude when I just ask for something.
Okay, I didn't ask. I just took them. But still.
Then in the evening I shouted at her when she came into my room, because I was tired from cricket practice and my knee hurt. That's different. I had a reason.
Mummy said, "Maybe Vidya had a reason too. She has boards tomorrow." I forgot about her boards.
So when I shout it's because I'm tired, and when she shouts it's because she's rude? Hmm. That doesn't seem fair when I write it down.
Hemant

qa.q: Why did Hemant shout at Vidya in the evening?
qa.a: Because Hemant was tired from cricket practice and the knee hurt.

qa.q: Why did Hemant decide Vidya is rude?
qa.a: Hemant felt hurt at being shouted at and didn't think about her boards, so it seemed like her character rather than her stress.

qa.q: What could Hemant do next time before calling someone rude?
qa.a: Ask, as Mummy did, whether they might have a reason too, like the reasons Hemant has for shouting.

qa.q: What might Vidya's day have been like?
qa.a: Vidya had boards the next day, so she was probably stressed, and her headphones had been taken without asking.

grounding: A child's diary shows excusing their own shouting as tiredness while calling a sister's shouting rudeness.

passage: At the Dussehra mela beside the village tank, the queue for the giant wheel was long and hot. Vijay's father had given him exactly one ticket and told him to be back by six for the Ravan burning. At 5:40 Vijay pushed past two boys to get ahead. "I have to be back by six," he muttered. "It's not my fault." Five minutes later, Akash from the next village elbowed past him too. "Hey!" Vijay shouted. "Bully! You think you own the queue!" Akash turned, panting. "My little sister is lost near the sweet stalls. I'm going to the loudspeaker man." Vijay stepped back and watched him run, suddenly aware of his own elbows.

qa.q: What time did Vijay have to be back?
qa.a: By six, for the Ravan burning.

qa.q: Why did Vijay call Akash a bully?
qa.a: He felt angry at being elbowed, so it seemed like Akash's nature, while his own pushing felt excused by the six o'clock deadline.

qa.q: What could Vijay learn from Akash's answer?
qa.a: That other people who push may have urgent reasons too, like a lost sister, just as Vijay had his deadline.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling as he pushed past?
qa.a: Akash was probably frightened and desperate, running to the loudspeaker man because his little sister was lost.

grounding: A boy excuses his own pushing at a fair by his deadline but calls another boy a bully, until he hears the boy's reason.

passage: Gabriel was late for the school bus in Lisbon, and when the bell rang he shoved past Tiago at the classroom door. "Sorry, I'm in a hurry!" he called over his shoulder. At lunch the canteen line was long. Tiago stepped back to let someone pass and knocked Gabriel's tray. Juice everywhere. "You did that because you're rude," Gabriel said. "You always push." That evening, telling his sister Beatriz about it, he said, "Tiago is so rude. He pushes everyone." Beatriz raised her eyebrows. "And this morning at the door?" "That was different. I was late for the bus." "So when you push, it's the bus. When Tiago pushes, it's Tiago?" Gabriel opened his mouth, then closed it and went to find his football.

qa.q: What did Tiago knock at lunch?
qa.a: Gabriel's tray.

qa.q: Why was Gabriel so annoyed with Tiago?
qa.a: Covered in juice, Gabriel felt angry and decided Tiago was simply rude, not noticing the long, crowded canteen line.

qa.q: What question helped Gabriel see his double standard, and what could he try next time?
qa.a: Beatriz asked about the morning push; next time Gabriel could look for a hurry or a crowd behind someone else's push, as he does for his own.

qa.q: How might Tiago see what happened in the canteen?
qa.a: Tiago probably saw it as an accident while stepping back to let someone pass, and felt unfairly called rude.

grounding: Shows a child explaining his own push by being in a hurry but calling another boy's push a sign that he is rude.

passage: The swimming club's changing room was steamy and packed after the Saturday class. Omkar, shivering, pushed ahead of Dorje to get to the warm shower. "I'm freezing," he said. Five minutes later, Dorje, dripping, bumped past Omkar at the lockers. "Hey! Stop pushing, you're so rude," Omkar snapped. Pema ma'am, the coach, was folding towels by the door. "Omkar, why did you push at the shower?" "Because I was cold!" "Why do you think Dorje pushed at the lockers?" "Because he's rude. He's always like that." "Is he always like that?" Omkar thought. Dorje had shared his goggles last week. "No..." "It's crowded, everyone's cold," Pema ma'am said. "Maybe Dorje is cold too." Omkar looked over. Dorje's lips were blue.

qa.q: Why did Omkar push ahead to the shower?
qa.a: Because he was cold; he was shivering and said, "I'm freezing."

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when Dorje bumped past him at the lockers?
qa.a: He felt irritated and quickly decided Dorje was rude, while he saw his own push as only about being cold.

qa.q: How did Pema ma'am help, and what could Omkar ask himself next time?
qa.a: She asked why each of them pushed; next time Omkar could ask whether the other child might be cold or rushed, just like him.

qa.q: What is it like for Dorje to be called rude in the changing room?
qa.a: Dorje was likely cold and hurrying too, so being called rude would feel unfair after sharing his goggles only last week.

grounding: Shows a child excusing his own push because he was cold while calling another child's push rude, in a crowded swimming-club changing room.

passage:
Monday. At the park gate, Hrithik pushed Bittu out of the way to reach the swing first. "I only had ten minutes before tuition!" he told Rashmi didi, his tutor.
Wednesday. Bittu pushed Hrithik at the slide. Hrithik stormed into tuition. "Bittu is such a rude boy. He has no manners." Rashmi didi only said, "Hmm. Write that down for me."
Saturday. Rashmi didi gave him a small worksheet. Two lines. "Monday: Hrithik pushed because ______." "Wednesday: Bittu pushed because ______." Hrithik filled the first quickly: "I was in a hurry." The second, he started to write "he is rude," and stopped. He thought about the slide queue. It had been long, and Bittu's mother was calling him home. He wrote, "maybe he was in a hurry too."

qa.q: How many minutes did Hrithik say he had before tuition on Monday?
qa.a: He said he only had ten minutes before tuition.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when he stormed into tuition on Wednesday?
qa.a: He felt angry and sure Bittu was simply a rude boy with no manners, forgetting his own push on Monday.

qa.q: How did Rashmi didi's worksheet help Hrithik?
qa.a: It put both pushes side by side, so he had to give Bittu a reason the same way he gave himself one.

qa.q: How might Bittu see the push at the slide?
qa.a: Bittu may have felt rushed because his mother was calling him home, not that he was being rude.

grounding: Shows over a week a child explaining his own push by hurry while calling another boy's push rude, until a worksheet puts them side by side.

passage:
Jasleen, you pushed Harpreet in the line and then said he was the rude one? Come, sit. Let your grandfather Tenzin tell you about Losar when I was nine.

On the first morning of the new year, all the children in our settlement lined up at the monastery for the sweet bread. I was late because I'd been looking for my new shoes. So I pushed through to the front. I told myself, I'm in a hurry, it's fine.

Then a boy called Dorje pushed past me. I shouted at him, "You're so rude!"

My mother asked me, "Why did Dorje push?" I couldn't say. "Why did you push?" I said, because I was late.

She said, "Maybe Dorje was late too."

So, Jasleen, why do you think Harpreet pushed?

qa.q: What were the children lining up for at the monastery?
qa.a: The sweet bread.

qa.q: Why did young Tenzin think Dorje was rude?
qa.a: Young Tenzin felt angry and read Dorje's push as bad character, while excusing his own push as just being in a hurry.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Tenzin's story?
qa.a: His mother asking why each of them pushed showed that Tenzin had a reason for himself but only judged Dorje's character.

qa.q: How might Dorje have felt being called rude?
qa.a: Dorje might have felt hurt and unfairly judged, maybe also hurrying for his own reasons.

grounding: An elder recalls excusing his own push at a festival as hurry while calling another boy rude.

passage:
It was the first school day after the Diwali holidays, and the bus was about to leave. Nilesh ran for the steps and shoved past a younger boy. "Sorry, I'm late!" he called over his shoulder.

At the top of the steps, Tushar pushed past him to grab the last window seat. Nilesh nearly fell.

"He's so rude," Nilesh told his friend as they sat down. "He always does that."

The friend looked at him. "You just pushed that little kid at the bottom."

"That's different. I was late."

"Maybe Tushar was scared of losing the window seat. He gets bus sick."

Nilesh looked at Tushar, who was pressing his forehead to the cold glass.

qa.q: Why did Tushar want the window seat?
qa.a: He gets bus sick.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh think Tushar was rude but excuse himself?
qa.a: Nilesh felt annoyed and saw his own push as caused by being late, while reading Tushar's push as bad character.

qa.q: What did Nilesh's friend say that helped?
qa.a: The friend reminded Nilesh he had just pushed a younger boy and offered a reason Tushar might have pushed, the bus sickness.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt on the bus?
qa.a: Tushar probably felt unwell and anxious, which is why he rushed for the window.

grounding: On a rushed school morning, a child excuses his own push as lateness but calls another child rude for pushing.

passage:
Christmas carol practice was in ten minutes, and the corridor outside the music room was crowded. Kiran pushed through to get to the front. "I'm late, sorry," he muttered.

A moment later, Shankar elbowed past him. Kiran glared. "He's so rude," he said to the girl next to him. "He never waits."

In the music room, the teacher asked, "Why were there so many pushes outside?"

Kiran put his hand up. "Shankar pushed me."

"And did you push anyone, Kiran?"

Kiran went red. "Yes, but I had a reason. I was late."

"Shankar, did you have a reason?"

"I had to set up the keyboard before we started, Miss."

The teacher looked at Kiran. "So you both had reasons. But you only gave yourself one."

Kiran looked at his shoes.

qa.q: Why did Shankar push past, according to him?
qa.a: I had to set up the keyboard before we started, Miss.

qa.q: Why did Kiran call Shankar rude?
qa.a: Kiran felt irritated and read Shankar's push as character, while he excused his own push as being late.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Kiran see the unfairness?
qa.a: The teacher asked both boys for their reasons, showing that Kiran only allowed a reason for himself.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt when Kiran said he pushed?
qa.a: Shankar may have felt unfairly accused, since he was hurrying to set up the keyboard.

grounding: During Christmas practice, a child excuses his own push as lateness but calls another boy rude.

passage:
Raksha Bandhan morning, and the bathroom door banged twice.
"Mumma! Gautam pushed me!"
"He pushed me first!"
Mumma came out of the kitchen with rakhi thread still in her hand. "Tarun, did you push him?"
"Only because I was late! Didi is coming at nine and I haven't even brushed."
"And why did Gautam push you?"
"Because he's rude. He's always rude."
Gautam folded his arms. "I was late too. My kurta's still in the cupboard."
"That's different," Tarun said.
"How is it different?" Mumma asked.
Tarun opened his mouth, then shut it. "Because mine was a reason."
Mumma laughed and handed them each a toothbrush. "You both had reasons. Brush together. Quickly."

qa.q: What time was Didi coming?
qa.a: Didi was coming at nine.

qa.q: Why does Tarun think his own push was different?
qa.a: Tarun feels his own rush from the inside, so his push seems fully explained, while Gautam's push feels rude and annoying because he can't see Gautam's hurry.

qa.q: What did Mumma's question help Tarun notice?
qa.a: Asking "How is it different?" made Tarun see that both of them were late, so neither push was really about being rude.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel when Tarun calls him rude?
qa.a: Gautam probably feels hurt and unfairly blamed, since he was also rushing to find his kurta.

grounding: Shows a child explaining his own push by being in a hurry while saying the other child pushed because he is rude.
